Circular and arc-like coordinates

Source: R/coord-circos.R
coord_circos.Rd

coord_circos() draws the panel in polar coordinates: x is the radius, y is the angle in radians. coord_arc() is the linear counterpart – nodes sit on a line and links bulge to one side. ggcircos() installs the right one for you; you rarely need to call these directly.

Usage

coord_circos(
  theta = "y",
  clockwise = TRUE,
  start = -pi/2,
  clip = "off",
  r.axis = FALSE,
  expand = c(FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE),
  limits = NULL,
  direction = NULL,
  ...
)

coord_arc(xlim = c(-1, 1), ylim = NULL, clip = "off", expand = FALSE, ...)

Arguments

theta

Which aesthetic holds the angle. Only "y" is supported.

clockwise

Direction of increasing theta on screen: TRUE puts theta = 0 at 12 o'clock and runs clockwise, FALSE runs counter-clockwise.

start

Angle (radians) of theta = 0 on the ring, measured clockwise from 12 o'clock. ggcircos() passes the layout's start here, so the first node lands where the layout says it does.

clip

Should the panel be clipped to its range? "off" by default so that bulging links are not cut off.

r.axis

Draw the radial axis. FALSE by default: a radius has no physical meaning here.

expand, limits, ...

Passed on to ggplot2::coord_radial() or ggplot2::coord_cartesian(). A plain numeric limits is read as the angle range: coord_circos(limits = c(0, 2 * pi)) says "the angle axis is the whole circle", which is what a hand-built plot needs (see vignette("from-circlize") and the layout-as-data section of vignette("tracks")).

direction

Rejected on purpose: the coord_polar() spelling for clockwise. Present in the signature so that old code gets a classed error instead of "unused argument".

xlim, ylim

Panel ranges for coord_arc().

Value

A ggplot2 coordinate.

Details

The circular coordinate is built on ggplot2::coord_radial(): the radius axis is suppressed (a radius has no physical meaning here), the angle is taken from y, and coord_circos() maps its own arguments onto the fields CoordRadial expects. Labels are rotated with the screen angle the coordinate itself reports, so they stay attached to the circle for any clockwise setting.

coord_arc() locks the radius unit to the angle unit (ratio = 1), because the linear layout has no circle to borrow a scale from: without it a chord spanning half a turn is drawn as a tall loop instead of an arc. The angle axis covers a whole turn, so this layout wants a tall device (roughly 1:2 or narrower); in a square device the panel becomes a narrow column.

Examples

# normally installed for you by ggcircos()
p <- ggplot2::ggplot(data.frame(x = 1, y = 0), ggplot2::aes(x, y)) +
    ggplot2::geom_point() +
    coord_circos()
p
#> Warning: The angle scale no longer spans `[0, 2*pi]`: labels and slots will sit in the
#> wrong place.
#> ℹ Leave the y scale of a ggcircos plot alone; the layout already fixed it to
#>   `c(0, 2*pi)`.
